meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I'm just tired.
It's easy.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

припугнуть.gloss: to scare a little, to give a fright

meanings.en: to scare a little, to give a fright
meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'пугнуть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to scare a little, to give a fright', paired with 'пугать'.

related.gloss: to to scare a little (prefixed perfective)
not to to scare a little (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Мы так его припугнём, и всё.
examples.trans: We'll just give him a scare, that's all.
He only wanted to scare his neighbour a bit.

examples.text: Кто тебя заставляет пытать, Самсон? Мы так его припугнём, и всё.
examples.trans: Who is making you torture anyone, Samson? We'll just give him a scare, that's all.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes, indeed', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh yeah?
Yes, it's me.
Oh yeah? When?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'the heck, away (colloq.)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What do you need the knife for?

examples.text: На кухне все стараются работать нафиг.
examples.trans: In the kitchen everyone tries to work the heck.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'knife' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Cutting a living person with a knife!
There is a sharp knife on the table.

examples.text: Нина, ну как ты могла? Живого человека ножом резать!
examples.trans: Nina, how could you? Cutting a living person with a knife!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

всякий.gloss: every kind of, all sorts of, any

meanings.en: every kind of, all sorts of, any
meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'який').

examples.trans: Alright, all sorts of things happen.
Take an umbrella just in case.

examples.text: Ладно, всякое бывает. Ну что вы?
examples.trans: Alright, all sorts of things happen. Oh, come on.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лучай'). Common masculine noun meaning 'case, occasion, incident' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Take it, just in case.
This is a strange case.

examples.text: Возьмите, пожалуйста. На случай, если передумаете.
examples.trans: Please take this. In case you change your mind.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'if', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Come if you want.
And if not?
Take her if you want.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'bread' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Buy some bread.
The bread is on the table.
Vodka is liquid bread.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'suddenly; all of a sudden', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Why did it suddenly draw level?
Suddenly it began to rain.

examples.text: Почему он вдруг сравнялся? Мы шли впереди на десять процентов!
examples.trans: Why did it suddenly draw level? We were ten percent ahead!

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: The boat suddenly hit a rock.

examples.text: Баржа внезапно наткнулась на что-то и стала тонуть.
examples.trans: The barge suddenly hit something and began to sink.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('necessary, needed').

examples.trans: I need a job too.
Do you need a pen?
He needs money.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'резать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to slice; to cut up', paired with 'нарезать'.

examples.text: Вот теперь кусочки нарезаны красиво и аккуратно.
examples.trans: Now the pieces are cut beautifully and neatly.

examples.text: Сначала мелко нарежь лук и морковь.
examples.trans: First chop the onion and carrot finely.
I will cut the vegetables into even pieces.

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'говорить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'we will finish talking'.

related.gloss: to we will finish talking (prefixed perfective)
not to we will finish talking (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Тихо, мы с тобой потом договорим.
examples.trans: Quiet, you and I will finish talking later.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и договорить вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and we will finish talking on time.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning '(emphasis) after all, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.
But you've still got some.
I told you: no.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to give; (imperative) let's', paired with 'дать'.

examples.trans: Let's talk.
He gives me a book.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'go, walk', paired with 'пойти'.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

examples.text: Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: That's why I'm running for a second term.

examples.text: А ты иди на биржу труда. Там есть работа.
examples.trans: You go to the job centre. There's work there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'joke' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: It's a joke.
What kind of jokes are these?
Normal jokes. Where's the money?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'ставить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to put, to set up', paired with 'ставить'.

examples.text: Заходите. Поставьте, пожалуйста, правую ногу на кровать.
examples.trans: Come in. Please put your right foot on the bed.

examples.text: Поставьте, пожалуйста, правую ногу на кровать.
examples.trans: Please put your right foot on the bed.
Tomorrow we'll put on a latch.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'nothing', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There's nothing left.
I don't know anything.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh, come on, Dad!
Well?

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Common Russian noun meaning 'kids; guys' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Тогда ребята с тобой поработают. До свидания, Аркадий Борисович.
examples.trans: Then the boys will have a little word with you. Goodbye, Arkady Borisovich.
Then the boys will have a little word with you.
Right, kids, go out of the room.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: Prefix 'во-' ('into, up') marks inward or upward movement (stem 'обще').

examples.trans: That's no problem at all.
I have no idea at all.

examples.text: Я человек чистый. Я вообще не вор.
examples.trans: I'm an honest man. I'm not a thief at all.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'исходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to happen, go on', paired with 'произойти'.

examples.trans: What is going on? I don't understand.
What is happening here?

examples.text: Мы не знаем, что с нашей дочерью происходит!
examples.trans: We don't know what is happening with our daughter!

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Quiet, the children are asleep!
It's quiet here.
Quiet, please.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'делать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'make, cause'.

examples.trans: What have you done, Victoria?

examples.text: Что, я зря пришла? Я надела костюм зайки!
examples.trans: What, did I come for nothing? I put on a bunny costume!

examples.text: Что ты наделал, ведь это мои деньги!
examples.trans: What have you done, after all that is my money!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: I want coffee.
If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'много'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I need to do a bit of work.
I'm a bit tired.

examples.text: Мы даём вам ещё немного времени.
examples.trans: We are giving you a little more time.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'what for, why', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What have you come for?
What's that for?
Oh, Samson. What have you come for?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Grab him!
It needs a wash.
Four-eyes! Grab him!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to touch', paired with 'тронуть'.

examples.trans: Don't touch me!
Don't touch the car.

examples.text: Всё, хорошо, я тебя выпущу! Только собаку не трогай!
examples.trans: All right, fine, I'll let you out! Just don't touch the dog!

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'дурок'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'fool, moron, jerk' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There are only morons around!

examples.text: Вокруг меня одни лентяи и придурки!
examples.trans: Around me are only slackers and fools!

examples.text: Ну ты и придурок, честное слово!
examples.trans: Well you are a jerk, honestly!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'let's go'.

examples.trans: Can I go and have a look?
Not allowed? All right, I'll go and do my homework.
All right, let's go to our room.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Share with everyone.
I'm with Dad.
Share it all equally with everyone, understand?
